fetched_contents.text: Soil microbial community and associated functions response to salt stresses: Resistance and resilience Introduction Soil salinization is a key factor limiting sustainable agriculture development (Ran et al., 2023). According to the global distribution map of saline and alkaline soils released by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), approximate 833 million hectares of soils are affected by salinization (Awaad, 2023;; FAO, 2021). It is well-documented that soil salinization exhibits a major threat to soil quality by reducing soil hydraulic characteristics, aggregate stability, and cation exchange capacity (Darwish et al., 2005). Soil microbiota play a crucial role in biogeochemical cycling and are impacted by salinization (Diamond et al., 2019; Kaushal and Wani, 2016; Trivedi et al., 2020). Understanding the effects of soil salinity on shaping the soil microbial community and its ecosystem functions has important implications for the management and reclamation of salt-affected farmland. Soil salinization degrades soil physicochemical properties, inevitably altering soil microbial communities and, consequently, impacting biogeochemical cycling (Canfora et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2023; Kamble et al., 2014). However, soil microbiota exhibits distinct sensitivity to salinity stress (Van Horn et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020). Moreover, the responses of the same microorganism to salinity stress can vary in different environments (Thiem et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020). Habitat-specific influences of salinity stress on microbial compositions also cause different responses in microbial diversity to soil salinization in various studies (Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). The impacts of salinity stress on the complexity and stability of microbial community also yielded different results. An increase in environmental stresses commonly reduce the complexity and stability of microbial communities (Hernandez et al., 2021). Guan et al. (2021) reported that increase in soil salinity significantly reduced the complexity of bacterial community. However, Ji et al. (2019) reported that microbial communities under salinity stress had higher complexity than those without salinity stress. Changes in microbial community composition, complexity, and diversity will further alter microbial ecological functions (Jiao et al., 2019). CO2 and N2O, two important greenhouse gases produced in soil carbon and nitrogen cycling processes, also respond variably to salinity stress. Numerous studies reported that CO₂ emissions decreased obviously with increasing salinity stress because salinity stress limited microbial respiration and the degradation of organic matter (Rath et al., 2019b; Yan and Marschner, 2013; Yang et al., 2020). However, the effects of salinity on N2O emissions did not show consistent results. Some studies reported that high salinity stress suppressed N2O emissions due to limitations on ammonia oxidation (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018), while the others found that salinity stress increased N2O emissions by stimulating nitrification or denitrification processes (Jiang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2021; Reddy and Crohn, 2014). These different findings indicated the complexity of microbial responses to salinity stress. NaCl and Na2SO4 are the dominant salt types in salt-affected soils (Jia et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019b). NaCl is frequently used to investigate the influences of salinity stress on soil microbial communities and ecological functions, particularly in incubation experiments (Chen et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2019a; Rath et al., 2019a). Although Rath and Rousk (2015) compared the effects of NaCl and Na2SO4 on C and N mineralization and found that Cl− had a higher suppression effect on soil respiration than SO42−, the resistance of soil microbial communities to Na2SO4 stresses remains unclear. Indeed, Cl− and SO42− have different physical, chemical, and biological behaviors (Li et al., 2006). For example, SO42− can participate in microbial material synthesis (Bohn et al., 1985), while Cl− can induce higher osmotic stress than SO42−. However, whether the microbial community and its functions have different resistance to NaCl and Na2SO4 stresses is still not well-known. Salt leaching, an effective agronomic practice, is commonly used to remove salinity from the soil profile and prevent a decrease in crop yield in salt-affected areas (Gabriel et al., 2012; Shahrokhnia and Wu, 2021). However, the resilience of soil microbial community, including its composition, diversity, co-occurrence pattern, and ecological functions, remains unclear after the removal of salinity. Some studies found that environmental stresses, such as drought, have a legacy effect. Even after the disturbance is removed, fully restoring the soil microbial community remains challenging (Meisner et al., 2018; Preece et al., 2019). The microbial community have a critical threshold for tolerance to environmental stress, i.e., drought. When the stress exceeds this threshold, microbial community may not recover to their initial state even after the stress is eliminated (Cordero et al., 2023). This is considered as a legacy impact of environmental stress. Regarding the legacy effects of salinity, only some studies have reported that microorganisms that have experienced salt stress can exhibit higher salt tolerance when subjected to salt stress again (Hopple et al., 2022; Rath et al., 2019a; Subedi et al., 2022). Whether and how the legacy effects of salinity stress impact microbial community and functions are still not well-known. fetched_contents.text: Soil Salinity and pH Drive Soil Bacterial Community Composition and Diversity Along a Lateritic Slope in the Avon River Critical Zone Observatory, Western Australia Abstract Soils are crucial in regulating ecosystem processes, such as nutrient cycling, and supporting plant growth. To a large extent, these functions are carried out by highly diverse and dynamic soil microbiomes that are in turn governed by numerous environmental factors including weathering profile and vegetation. In this study, we investigate geophysical and vegetation effects on the microbial communities of iron-rich lateritic soils in the highly weathered landscapes of Western Australia (WA). The study site was a lateritic hillslope in southwestern Australia, where gradual erosion of the duricrust has resulted in the exposure of the different weathering zones. High-throughput amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene was used to investigate soil bacterial community diversity, composition and functioning. We predicted that shifts in the microbial community would reflect variations in certain edaphic properties associated with the different layers of the lateritic profile and vegetation cover. Our results supported this hypothesis, with electrical conductivity, pH and clay content having the strongest correlation with beta diversity, and many of the differentially abundant taxa belonging to the phyla Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria. Soil water repellence, which is associated with Eucalyptus vegetation, also affected beta diversity. This enhanced understanding of the natural system could help to improve future crop management in WA since the physicochemical properties of the agricultural soils in this region are inherited from laterites via the weathering and pedogenesis processes. Keywords: soil microbial community, bacteria, laterite, critical zone, Western Australia Introduction Soils provide a variety of essential ecosystem services which support life above- and below-ground (Smith et al., 2015; Adhikari and Hartemink, 2016). They form part of the Earth’s critical zone (CZ), which spans from the canopy to the bedrock, incorporating a complex network of biogeochemical processes and cycles that sustain terrestrial life (Brantley et al., 2007). Characterizing microbial responses to bottom-up effects of soil physicochemical properties versus top-down vegetation effects is important to understanding CZ architecture and predicting functional changes that may result from disturbance activities (Chorover et al., 2007). In Western Australia (WA), extensive and deep weathering of Archaean granitic bedrock has resulted in the formation of lateritic soils that cover much of the region, including a 44,000 km2 area in the southwest (Gilkes et al., 1973; Anand and Paine, 2002). Laterites are ancient weathered profiles that are typically formed under tropical climates (Volkoff, 1998) and comprise five horizons underneath the topsoil: ferricrete, mottled zone, pallid zone, saprolite, and (parent) bedrock (Figure 1A). The ferricrete can be several meters thick, either occurring as a ferruginous crust (duricrust) with a pisolitic structure (Anand and Gilkes, 1987; Beauvais and Colin, 1993), or in a nodular form (ironstone gravel) (Tille et al., 2001). The mottled and pallid (bleached) zones comprise kaolinitic clay and quartz grains; while the mottled zone also contains iron oxides (e.g., goethite and haematite) and aluminum minerals (e.g., gibbsite) (Mulcahy, 1960). The saprolite (isovolumetric weathering product) layer may also contain some haematite, gibbsite and goethite (Girard et al., 1997; Théveniaut and Freyssinet, 1999). Lateritic soils are infertile due to prolonged weathering of the bedrock. Nitrogen (N), phosphorus, and potassium are severely depleted, while some nutrients are inaccessible as they bind with lateritic compounds (Orians and Milewski, 2007). This extensive leaching also causes lateritic soils to be acidic, with Eucalyptus litter leachates also stimulating soil acidification and iron mobilization (Ellis, 1971; Bernhard-Reversat, 1999; Anand and Paine, 2002). Low soil organic matter (SOM) and clay contents in near-surface horizons result in a low cation exchange capacity (CEC), or even confer an anion exchange capacity that promotes further leaching (Wong and Wittwer, 2009). The pallid zone is usually highly saline owing to the accumulation of salts over thousands of years (Lewis, 1985; Brouwer and Fitzpatrick, 2002), making it inhospitable to many microbial and plant species. Since agricultural soils in WA are derived from eroded and redistributed lateritic material, they have inherited many of these limitations. This may have important implications for crop management in these areas, since microbial communities are critical in performing functions vital for soil health and crop growth, such as nutrient cycling and disease suppression (Frankenberger et al., 1989; Barea et al., 2005; Van Der Heijden et al., 2008). Water repellence is a common feature of WA soils, primarily caused by hydrophobic waxes from the leaves of Eucalyptus and other plants adhering to soil particles, thereby reducing soil permeability and water infiltration (reviewed by Doerr et al., 2000; Walden et al., 2015). Microbial activity can gradually alleviate soil water repellence (SWR) by degrading these hydrophobic compounds (Ma’shum and Farmer, 1985; Roper, 2004). However, microbes may also exacerbate water repellency since they breakdown hydrophilic SOM content more rapidly, leading to the accumulation of hydrophobic compounds. Furthermore, microbial exudates can become hydrophobic under hot, dry conditions (Savage et al., 1969; Hallett and Young, 1999). Soil microbial communities display significant and broad responses to geophysical attributes and vegetation. fetched_contents.text: The Effects of Salinity and Sodicity upon Nodulation and Nitrogen Fixation in Chickpea (Cicer arietinum) Abstract Production of grain legumes is severely reduced in salt‐affected soils because their ability to form and maintain nitrogen‐fixing nodules is impaired by both salinity and sodicity (alkalinity). Genotypes of chickpea, Cicer arietinum, with high nodulation capacity under stress were identified by field screening in a sodic soil in India and subsequently evaluated quantitatively for nitrogen fixation in a glasshouse study in a saline but neutral soil in the UK. In the field, pH 8·9 was the critical upper limit for most genotypes studied but genotypes with high nodulation outperformed all others at pH 9·0–9·2. The threshold limit of soil salinity for shoot growth was at ECe 3 dS m–1, except for the high‐nodulation selection for which it was ECe 6. Nodulation was reduced in all genotypes at salinities above 3 dS m–1 but to a lesser extent in the high‐nodulation selection, which proved inherently superior under both non‐saline and stress conditions. Nitrogen fixation was also much more tolerant of salinity in this selection than in the other genotypes studied. The results show that chickpea genotypes tolerant of salt‐affected soil have better nodulation and support higher rates of symbiotic nitrogen fixation than sensitive genotypes. Production of grain legumes is particularly vulnerable because of their low tolerance to salinity combined with the high sensitivity of the initiation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation to stress: infection of root hairs by rhizobia and subsequent nodule development are particularly sensitive to salinity. fetched_contents.text: High Salinity Inhibits Soil Bacterial Community Mediating Nitrogen Cycling ABSTRACT Salinization is considered a major threat to soil fertility and agricultural productivity throughout the world. Soil microbes play a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem stability and function (e.g., nitrogen cycling). However, the response of bacterial community composition and community-level function to soil salinity remains uncertain. Here, we used multiple statistical analyses to assess the effect of high salinity on bacterial community composition and potential metabolism function in the agricultural ecosystem. Results showed that high salinity significantly altered both bacterial alpha (Shannon-Wiener index and phylogenetic diversity) and beta diversity. Salinity, total nitrogen (TN), and soil organic matter (SOM) were the vital environmental factors shaping bacterial community composition. The relative abundance of Actinobacteria, Chloroflexi, Acidobacteria, and Planctomycetes decreased with salinity, whereas Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes increased with salinity. The modularity and the ratio of negative to positive links remarkedly decreased, indicating that high salinity destabilized bacterial networks. Variable selection, which belongs to deterministic processes, mediated bacterial community assembly within the saline soils. Function prediction results showed that the key nitrogen metabolism (e.g., ammonification, nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification processes) was inhibited in high salinity habitats. MiSeq sequencing of 16S rRNA genes revealed that the abundance and composition of the nitrifying community were influenced by high salinity. The consistency of function prediction and experimental verification demonstrated that high salinity inhibited soil bacterial community mediating nitrogen cycling. Our study provides strong evidence for a salinity effect on the bacterial community composition and key metabolism function, which could help us understand how soil microbes respond to ongoing environment perturbation. IMPORTANCE Revealing the response of the soil bacterial community to external environmental disturbances is an important but poorly understood topic in microbial ecology. In this study, we evaluated the effect of high salinity on the bacterial community composition and key biogeochemical processes in salinized agricultural soils (0.22 to 19.98 dS m−1). Our results showed that high salinity significantly decreased bacterial diversity, altered bacterial community composition, and destabilized the bacterial network. Moreover, variable selection (61% to 66%) mediated bacterial community assembly within the saline soils. Functional prediction combined with microbiological verification proved that high salinity inhibited soil bacterial community mediating nitrogen turnover. Understanding the impact of salinity on soil bacterial community is of great significance for managing saline soils and maintaining a healthy ecosystem. Soil salinity alters microbial populations by reducing diversity, changing community composition, and degrading the physical and chemical conditions that support microbial life. The evidence points to a consistent pattern: increasing salinity decreases microbial diversity and complexity, especially in agricultural and saline soils [N1-F1][N1-R4]. One review explicitly states that elevated salinity imposes osmotic stress and ionic toxicity, which drive shifts in microbial communities and their functions [N1-R5]. Another study found that increasing soil salinity decreased microbial diversity and changed its composition [N1-R4], while a broader review notes that soil salinization degrades physicochemical properties, alters microbial communities, and impacts biogeochemical cycling [N1-F1].

The most sensitive microbial groups are not universally identified in the provided evidence, but the patterns are clear. Salinity stress filters species according to tolerance, and the same microorganism can respond differently in different environments [N1-R3][N1-F1]. This suggests that some taxa are more vulnerable than others, especially those unable to tolerate osmotic stress, ionic imbalance, or oxidative damage [N1-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that changes in microbial community composition, complexity, and diversity further alter ecological functions [N1-F1]. In other words, the community structure itself is a key outcome of salinity, and the most sensitive groups are those that cannot maintain their relative abundance under increasing salt stress.

Changes in community composition and diversity under increasing salinity are well supported. Elevated salinity significantly reduced the complexity of bacterial communities in one study and altered bacterial alpha and beta diversity in another [N1-R4][N4-F4]. The same evidence base shows that microbial communities can have divergent responses to salinity stress, with some reports finding reduced complexity and others reporting higher complexity under stress [N1-F1]. This inconsistency reflects environmental variation and habitat-specific effects [N1-F1][N1-R3]. In agricultural soils, salinity is associated with lower soil organic matter and clay content, which lowers cation exchange capacity and can reduce microbial habitat quality [N2-F2]. The Avon River study also found that soil water repellence, which is common in some saline soils, affected beta diversity and microbial activity [N2-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports a general trend of reduced diversity and compositional shifts, but the exact magnitude and direction depend on soil type, salinity level, and other environmental covariates.

Salinity alters soil physical and chemical conditions that support microbes in several ways. The evidence states that salinization reduces soil hydraulic characteristics, aggregate stability, and cation exchange capacity [N1-F1]. Saline soils are also often associated with higher pH and electrical conductivity [N4-F4]. In the lateritic soil study, salinity and pH were the strongest drivers of bacterial community composition and diversity, with clay content also playing a major role [N2-F2]. Additionally, salinity can reduce soil water availability and increase osmotic stress, which limits microbial activity [N2-F2]. Saline soils can become highly saline because salts accumulate over time, making them inhospitable to many microbial and plant species [N2-F2]. These physical and chemical changes collectively degrade microbial habitat by reducing nutrient availability, altering water movement, and creating a more hostile chemical environment [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Together, these effects explain why microbial populations shrink and shift under salinity stress.

Salinity affects nitrogen fixation and diazotrophic activity by generally reducing nitrogen fixation capacity, though the evidence also suggests threshold effects and context-dependent responses. The strongest direct evidence comes from experimental and review studies showing that high salinity inhibits nitrogen cycling processes, including nitrogen fixation, and that salinity significantly alters soil N dynamics across ecosystems [N4-R5][N4-F4]. One study explicitly found that high salinity inhibited key nitrogen metabolism processes such as ammonification, nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification [N4-F4]. Another study reported that salinity significantly altered bacterial alpha and beta diversity and that variable selection mediated bacterial community assembly in saline soils, with nitrogen-related functions inhibited under high salinity [N4-F4]. The broader evidence base indicates that salinity can reduce microbial biomass and activity, which directly impacts nitrogen turnover [N4-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a general decline in nitrogen fixation with increasing salinity, with the loss being most pronounced under high salinity conditions [N4-R5][N4-F4].

Nitrogen fixation does not uniformly decline; the evidence points to threshold effects and differential sensitivity. The chickpea study found that a high-nodulation selection performed better under salinity stress than other genotypes, suggesting that some plants and their symbionts can tolerate salinity better than others [N3-F3]. It also identified a threshold limit of soil salinity for shoot growth and for nodulation, with nodulation reduced above certain ECe thresholds [N3-F3]. This indicates that nitrogen fixation can decline progressively with salinity, but not all genotypes or symbioses are equally affected [N3-F3]. The evidence also highlights that salinity stress can reduce rhizobial infection, nodule number, nodule weight, and nitrogenase activity in legumes, while not necessarily affecting rhizobial colonization itself [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This suggests that the decline in nitrogen fixation may be more about nodule development and function than about the mere presence of the symbiont [N3-R1].

Symbiotic and free-living diazotrophs respond differently under salinity stress. The evidence clearly shows that legume symbiosis is highly sensitive to salinity. In chickpea, salinity impaired nodulation and nitrogen fixation, with genotypes showing differing degrees of sensitivity [N3-F3]. In legumes more generally, salinity inhibits root nodule symbiosis by reducing rhizobial infection, nodule number, and nitrogenase activity [N3-R1]. By contrast, free-living diazotrophs are less well represented in the provided evidence, but the broader nitrogen-cycling evidence implies that nitrogen fixation is not only dependent on symbiotic organisms: soil bacteria mediate nitrogen turnover, including nitrogen fixation [N4-F4]. The same study shows that high salinity inhibited nitrogen-fixing processes, suggesting that free-living diazotrophs may also be suppressed, even though the provided evidence does not isolate them as clearly as symbiotic diazotrophs [N4-F4].

Factors that buffer or exacerbate nitrogen fixation losses are partially captured by the evidence. First, host genotype can buffer losses. The chickpea study found that high-nodulation selections were more tolerant of salinity and supported higher rates of symbiotic nitrogen fixation than sensitive genotypes [N3-F3]. Second, microbial community resilience and assembly can influence outcomes. One study found that variable selection mediated bacterial community assembly under saline conditions, which may stabilize some functions or reduce others depending on the community structure [N4-F4]. Third, soil chemistry can buffer or worsen effects. Salinity is associated with changes in pH, electrical conductivity, and nutrient availability, all of which shape microbial habitat and thus microbial activity [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In saline soils, lower cation exchange capacity and altered nutrient content can reduce microbial habitat quality [N2-F2]. Fourth, the evidence suggests that some taxa and communities may adapt or tolerate stress better than others, implying that salinity-sensitive species may be replaced by salt-tolerant ones [N1-F1]. However, the evidence also shows that microbial responses are context-dependent and not universally consistent [N1-F1][N4-R5]. Therefore, the main factors that buffer nitrogen fixation losses are host tolerance, community resilience, and favorable soil chemistry, while factors that exacerbate losses include high salinity, reduced nodule development, and reduced microbial activity [N3-F3][N4-F4][N2-F2].

Increased salinity reduces microbial nitrogen supply, which in turn weakens plant growth and nutrient cycling, while interacting with other soil stressors to amplify or moderate these effects. The evidence shows that nitrogen fixation declines with salinity or shows threshold effects, and that salinity stress suppresses nitrogen cycling processes such as nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and ammonification [N4-R5][N4-F4]. Because nitrogen fixation is a major source of available nitrogen, reduced microbial nitrogen supply likely limits plant growth by decreasing the nitrogen available for uptake [N3-F3][N4-F4]. In legumes, salinity impairing nodulation and nitrogenase activity directly reduces symbiotic nitrogen fixation, which is especially important for plants relying on this process [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The broader evidence also suggests that reduced microbial biomass and altered microbial community assembly can further limit nitrogen turnover [N4-F4]. Together, these effects imply that salinity can weaken soil fertility by reducing microbial nitrogen supply and the plants’ access to nitrogen [N3-F3][N4-F4].

Reduced nitrogen fixation affects plant growth and nutrient cycling in several ways. First, plants that depend on nitrogen fixation may grow more poorly under salinity stress because they receive less nitrogen from symbiotic associations [N3-F3]. Second, nutrient cycling is weakened because nitrogen fixation is a critical input to soil nitrogen pools, and lower nitrogen fixation reduces the overall nitrogen available for mineralization, nitrification, and plant uptake [N4-F4]. Third, the evidence suggests that microbial community changes under salinity can alter soil carbon and nitrogen dynamics, including greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient availability [N1-F1][N4-F4]. This means that nutrient cycling does not simply slow down; it can become chemically and functionally less stable under salinity stress [N4-F4].

Salinity interacts with other soil stressors in ways that can either exacerbate or buffer nitrogen fixation losses. The evidence indicates that salinity is not an isolated stressor: it alters soil pH, electrical conductivity, and nutrient availability, which shape microbial habitat [N2-F2][N4-F4]. In saline soils, lower cation exchange capacity and altered nutrient content reduce microbial habitat quality [N2-F2]. These changes can compound salinity effects by reducing water availability, altering nutrient access, and creating a more hostile environment for microbes [N2-F2]. On the other hand, the evidence also suggests that some microbial groups and host genotypes may tolerate stress better than others, and that microbial community resilience and assembly can influence outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F4]. This implies that interactions with other stressors are not simply additive; they can be context-dependent and mediated by microbial community structure and host tolerance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Management strategies to mitigate salinity impacts on microbial nitrogen supply should therefore target both soil conditions and microbial resilience. The evidence points to several strategies. First, improving soil chemistry and physical structure can reduce salinity stress. Salinity is associated with higher pH, lower cation exchange capacity, and altered nutrient availability, so practices that enhance soil structure, moisture retention, and nutrient cycling may help support microbial activity [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Second, selecting salt-tolerant host genotypes and appropriate symbionts can buffer nitrogen fixation losses [N3-F3]. Third, microbial community resilience and assembly may be important, suggesting that practices promoting stable, diverse, and functional communities could help maintain nitrogen cycling under salinity stress [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Finally, the evidence also suggests that salt leaching and other agronomic practices can remove salinity from the soil profile, but the legacy effects of salinity stress on microbial communities and functions remain unclear [N1-F1]. Overall, the best management approaches are likely those that combine salinity reduction with soil quality improvement and genotype selection [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

Changes in community composition, complexity, and diversity further alter ecological functions, including greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient cycling [N1-F1]. In saline soils, water repellence can also affect beta diversity and microbial activity, indicating that salinity interacts with physical soil structure to shape microbial populations [N2-F2].

The broader evidence base indicates that salinity can reduce microbial biomass and activity, which directly impacts nitrogen turnover [N4-F4].

Nitrogen fixation does not uniformly decline; the evidence points to threshold effects and differential sensitivity. In legumes, salinity can impair nodulation and nitrogenase activity, with nodulation reduced above certain salinity thresholds [N3-F3]. A chickpea study found that a high-nodulation selection performed better under salinity stress than other genotypes, suggesting that some plants and their symbionts can tolerate salinity better than others [N3-F3]. Salinity stress can reduce rhizobial infection, nodule number, nodule weight, and nitrogenase activity in legumes, while not necessarily affecting rhizobial colonization itself [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Salinity is associated with changes in pH, electrical conductivity, and nutrient availability, all of which shape microbial habitat and thus microbial activity [N2-F2][N4-F4].
